title: Comparatives II — Intensifiers & Double Comparatives
subtitle: Make comparisons stronger, softer, or show two things changing together.
objectives: Strengthen a comparison with much, far, a lot, way
Soften a comparison with slightly, a bit, a little
Use double comparatives to show two things increasing or decreasing together
Use as...as and nowhere near as...as for comparisons of equality and clear inequality

content.intro: You already know how to form comparatives (taller, more interesting). Now let's control exactly how big the difference is, and how to link two comparisons together.

rules.heading: a) Strengthening a comparative
rules.body:
much / far / a lot / way (informal) + comparative — for a big difference.

  • This phone is much more expensive than that one.
  • She's far more experienced than her colleagues.
  • Today is way colder than yesterday. (informal)

rules.heading: b) Softening a comparative
rules.body:
slightly / a bit / a little + comparative — for a small difference.

  • This route is slightly longer, but it's more scenic.
  • I'm feeling a little better today.

rules.heading: c) Double comparatives
rules.body:
the + comparative..., the + comparative... — shows two things changing together.

  • The more you practice, the better you get.
  • The sooner we leave, the sooner we'll arrive.
  • The older I get, the less I worry about small things.

rules.heading: d) as...as and nowhere near as...as
rules.body:
as + adjective + as for equality; not as...as for inequality; nowhere near as...as for a big, clear difference.

  • This test was as difficult as the last one. (equal)
  • This test wasn't as difficult as the last one. (less difficult)
  • This test was nowhere near as difficult as the last one. (much less difficult — a strong contrast)

examples: The new stadium is much bigger than the old one.
She sings far better than I do.
This coffee is slightly stronger than usual.
He's a bit taller than his brother.
The more you read, the more you learn.
The harder you work, the luckier you get.
This city isn't as expensive as London.
The results were nowhere near as good as we expected.
This laptop is way faster than my old one.
The earlier you book, the cheaper the tickets are.

commonMistakes.wrong: This phone is very more expensive.
commonMistakes.right: This phone is much more expensive. / This phone is a lot more expensive.
commonMistakes.why: "Very" doesn't intensify comparatives — use much/far/a lot instead.

commonMistakes.wrong: The more you practice, better you get.
commonMistakes.right: The more you practice, the better you get.
commonMistakes.why: Both halves of a double comparative need "the" before the comparative form.

commonMistakes.wrong: This city is more expensive as London.
commonMistakes.right: This city is as expensive as London. / This city is more expensive than London.
commonMistakes.why: Don't mix the two patterns — "as...as" for equality, "more...than" for a one-way comparison, never "more...as."

commonMistakes.wrong: The exam was slightly more difficult a lot.
commonMistakes.right: The exam was slightly more difficult.
commonMistakes.why: Use only one intensifier at a time — don't combine a softener (slightly) with a strengthener (a lot).

commonMistakes.wrong: It's nowhere as difficult than the last one.
commonMistakes.right: It's nowhere near as difficult as the last one.
commonMistakes.why: The full expression is "nowhere near as...as," not "nowhere as...than."

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with much, slightly, the, or as, as appropriate.

items.prompt: This restaurant is ___ more expensive than the one downtown. (choose: much / slightly / very — pick the one that intensifies a comparative)
items.explanation: "Much" (or far/a lot) intensifies a comparative; "very" does not.

items.prompt: ___ sooner you tell me, ___ sooner I can help.
items.explanation: Double comparatives need "the" before each comparative form.

items.prompt: Her new apartment is ___ bigger — just a tiny bit more space.
items.explanation: "Slightly" softens the comparison for a small difference.

items.prompt: This coffee isn't ___ strong ___ the one I had yesterday.
___ harder you train, ___ stronger you become.
items.explanation: Double comparative pattern: the + comparative, the + comparative.

items.incorrect: This test is very more difficult than the last one.
answer: This test is much more difficult than the last one.
This test is a lot more difficult than the last one.
items.explanation: "Very" can't intensify a comparative — use much/far/a lot.

items.incorrect: The more you wait, worse it gets.
answer: The more you wait, the worse it gets.
items.explanation: Both halves of the double comparative need "the."

items.incorrect: This city is more crowded as São Paulo.
answer: This city is more crowded than São Paulo.
This city is as crowded as São Paulo.
items.explanation: Don't mix "more" with "as" — use "more...than" or "as...as," not "more...as."

items.incorrect: It's nowhere as good than I expected.
answer: It's nowhere near as good as I expected.
items.explanation: The correct phrase is "nowhere near as...as."

exercises.title: Guided Production
exercises.instructions: Write your own sentence for each prompt. There's no single correct answer — a model answer is shown for comparison after you submit.

items.prompt: Write one sentence with a double comparative (the + comparative, the + comparative) about something true for you.
items.modelAnswer: The more I practice English, the more confident I feel.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using “much” or “far” to strengthen a comparison between two things you know.
items.modelAnswer: My current job is far more interesting than my last one.

items.prompt: Write one sentence using “nowhere near as...as” to make a strong contrast.
items.modelAnswer: This year's winter was nowhere near as cold as last year's.

summary: Strengthen a comparative with much/far/a lot, never “very.”
Soften a comparative with slightly/a bit/a little.
Double comparatives (the + comparative, the + comparative) show two things changing together.
As...as = equal; not as...as = less; nowhere near as...as = a big, clear difference.
